extracted.intended_audience: physicians, professional masseurs, and informed general readers interested in therapeutic massage
extracted.subtask_description: Practical instructions and standards for performing therapeutic massage: selection of maneuvers (friction, manipulation, percussion, passive/assistive/resistive movements), regional division of the body, correct force, rates, sequencing, indications, contraindications, and physiological rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-and-return (longitudinal) friction preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: A slight deviation from the purely upward-strong method is advantageous: upward strokes of friction should generally be stronger, with the returning or downward movement lightly grazing the surface, imparting a soothing influence without retarding circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to a carpenter's plane: prefer longitudinal (along limb axis) and circular friction; avoid transverse friction at right angles as ungraceful and theoretical. Use palmar surface of fingers fitting into phalangeal depressions. Rate for double strokes: 100–150 per minute. Apply over convenient territories such as fingers to wrist for starting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of heel of hand for vigorous friction
rubrics_metrics.description: The heel of the hand should be used for especially vigorous friction of the palm and for the sole of the foot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For vigorous work on palmar surface or soles, apply heel of hand. For larger limbs, use straight-line and circular friction between joints; upward stroke must be kept within limits of chafing the skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional division and stroke rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the body into convenient bounded territories (e.g., fingers to wrist; wrist to elbow; elbow to shoulder; ankle to knee; knee to thigh; spine regions) and apply strokes joint-to-joint for each region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended stroke rates: fingers double strokes 100–150/min; circular/oval friction with both hands 250–500/min (combined); below-knee strokes 100–160/min each hand; above-knee 75–100/min; back/thighs slower (approx. 60–75/min each hand for medium-sized person) because skin is thicker and strokes are longer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular (oval) friction technique and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular friction in an oval form with both hands moving simultaneously—one ascending as the other descends—is highly serviceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate: 125–250 per minute with each hand, or 250–500 per minute with both. Each stroke should reach from joint to joint; keep upward stroke within limits of chafing the skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust force to skin and underlying tissues
rubrics_metrics.description: The force used in doing friction is intended to act upon the skin only; excessive force is often much greater than necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If redness/irritation are desired measures, coarser implements (towel, hair mitten, brush) would produce more effect than the hand. Force must be graduated to avoid bruising or chafing; when skin is cold/dry or tissues poorly nourished, inunction may be helpful but does not require special skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation/kneading (deep massage) principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulation (kneading, deep-rubbing) is done by adapting fingers and hands to the part without allowing them to slip, kneading/rolling/manipulating tissues from insertion toward origin, from extremities to trunk, in direction of returning blood and lymph currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use same surface divisions as friction. For finger malaxation (e.g., on fingers): place thumb parallel and index at right angles, compress and rotate at 75–150/min. Each grasped part may receive 3–4 manipulations before moving on; advance so areas overlap by half. Force must be carefully graduated: too great compresses/bruises, too light slips, gliding with strong compression chafes. Greasy substances can prevent chafing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic overlap and area progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance and review should be systematically carried on, overlapping each newly treated area by about one-half of the previously treated area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part included in a single grasp may receive several manipulations (3–4) before proceeding; this systematic progression applies to all tissues amenable to massage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stretching tissues in opposite directions (esp. joint flexures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to stretch the tissues in opposite directions at the same time, especially at flexures of joints where the skin is delicate and sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such procedures lead to sensation of tearing; let the elasticity (or lack of it) in the patient's tissues guide the practitioner to obtain normal stretch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended manipulation rates by region
rubrics_metrics.description: Rates of manipulative manoeuvres vary by region depending on tissue size and density.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arms: 75–150 per hand per minute; legs: 60–90 per hand per minute; thighs: 40–80 per hand per minute (thighs require more force due to larger muscles and dense fascia lata). Back manipulations about 60 per minute each hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid including subcutaneous bony surfaces in vigorous grasp
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcutaneous bony surfaces (e.g., tibia, ulna) incidentally get attention during manipulation, but including them in a vigorous grasp causes unnecessary discomfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place fingers appropriately; avoid placing thumb and fingers of one hand too near each other to prevent cramped movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back-specific technique and smoothness
rubrics_metrics.description: On the back, direct manipulations from the base of the skull downward, stretching tissues away from the spinal column and manipulating in graceful curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ends of fingers to roll muscles on each side of the spinal column, massage supra-spinous ligament with transverse to-and-fro movements, and apply up-and-down motions parallel to the spine in tissues between spinous and transverse processes. Avoid pushing, jerky movements; prefer smooth, uniform motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chest and abdomen: gentleness and colon-directed kneading
rubrics_metrics.description: Chest and abdomen tolerate gentler manipulation than back/limbs; use palms for moderate pressure, rolling/grasping skin and superficial fascia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the abdomen, perform steady, firm, deep kneading in the direction of the ascending, transverse, and descending colon; use heel of hand on the side nearest operator and fingers on the other side; avoid pressing simultaneously on anterior pelvis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common operator errors and economy of effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Many manipulators wrongly fix upper-arm/shoulder muscles instead of working from wrists and hands, thereby moving patient, tiring themselves, compressing patient's tissues and defeating massage objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work from the wrists and concentrate energy in muscles of hands and forearms so movements are economical and comfortable for both operator and patient; cultivation is the economy of effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine modalities and session structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Friction and manipulation can be used alternately and varied with rapid pinching, deeper grasping of subcutaneous tissue, percussion, and passive/assistive/resistive movements; finish one surface before moving to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sessions typically occupy 1/2 hour to an hour for all or part of these procedures. Pinching to excite circulation: 100–125/min per hand. To act on subcutaneous tissue, grasp a handful of skin and roll/stretch more slowly. Mobile intermittent compression is used for deeper, momentary grasping of muscles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percussion: methods, applicability, and rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Percussion applies only over muscular masses and can be done in various ways, ranked in relative importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order of methods: (1) ulnar borders of hands and fingers, (2) same with fingers separated, (3) ends of fingers with tips united, (4) dorsum of upper halves of fingers loosely flexed, (5) palms, (6) ulnar borders tightly shut, (7) palms concave compressing air. India-rubber air-balls on handles provide rapid percussion (250–600 blows/min with both).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial passive, resistive, assistive, and vigorous passive movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive motion, resistive motion, assistive movements, and vigorous passive motion each have distinct purposes and limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know joint anatomy and natural limits. Passive motion should be pushed until slight resistance felt; resistive movements should keep opposing force within patient's strength and stop short of fatigue. Assistive movements supplement weak patient effort to produce movement and can progressively strengthen a muscle. Vigorous passive motion may be used to break adhesions (specialized technique). Use spring-balance to estimate partial loss of motion or resistive capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indications, patient selection, and contraindications
rubrics_metrics.description: Massage requires some latent patient energy; patients who are too weak may be harmed. Techniques should be selected per individual needs; physician advice is advisable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not give friction where capillary circulation is already good; avoid passive/resistive movements in fatigued patients. Percussion helps rouse cold skin and flabby muscle and alternates with friction/manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological effects and therapeutic aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Massage mechanically empties veins and lymphatics, increases local circulation, favors absorption of products, stimulates vaso-motor nerves, and imitates benefits of exercise without exertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermittent compression causes arterial dilatation above pressure site and promotes onward rush of blood when released. Massage rouses dormant capillaries, increases interchange between blood and tissues, aids nutrition, and may help functional and organic heart disease by lessening peripheral resistance. It is tonic, sedative, and physiologically counter-irritant; relieves constipation, pain, stiffness, and induces relaxation/sleep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient breathing to assist lymphatic/venous flow
rubrics_metrics.description: While undergoing massage, patients should take frequent and deep inspirations to favor the flow of venous and lymphatic currents to the thorax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is often instinctive and aids the feeling of relief and lightness afterwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fascia and lymph-spaces role in absorption
rubrics_metrics.description: Stretching and relaxing fascia and lymph-spaces (by passive movement or massage) promotes absorption and onward flow of lymph into lymphatic vessels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental evidence (fascial stretching, injection studies) shows coloring matter penetrates lymph-spaces when fascia is alternately stretched and relaxed; thus passive motions and massage assist removal of effete matters from tissues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical observations and cultural techniques (lomi-lomi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional techniques such as Sandwich-Islanders' lomi-lomi (series of intermittent squeezes toward extremities) can produce powerful restorative effects and illustrate that various forms of tissue stirring often help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lomi-lomi may hinder returning circulation transiently and can fatten subjects; shows massage's benefits depend on operator skill and that some massage is often better than none. Be aware initial sessions may be disagreeable until tissues soften.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physician guidance and individualize treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and omit maneuvers according to individual case needs and seek physician advice where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: percussion to rouse circulation in cold skin; avoid unnecessary procedures (wasting time and strength) in cases not likely to benefit. The relative importance of procedures varies per case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jerky, pushing movements; prefer smooth uniform motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Too frequent error among practitioners is making pushing, jerky movements instead of smooth, uniform motions in each direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smoothness improves efficacy and comfort; jerky movements can produce discomfort and reduce benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and monitoring of progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simple objective measures when applicable (e.g., spring-balance to estimate partial loss of motion or resistive motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding a limb suspended in a cloth attached to a spring-balance shows weight reduction during patient's effort; spring-balance can also estimate resistive motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Session duration guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Time to occupy per combined procedures for a convenient surface or limb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full session with friction, manipulation, percussion, and remedial movements may occupy from half an hour to an hour for all or part of these procedures.
